newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, NATO seek breakthrough on future ties.
newsitem.headline: Russia, NATO seek breakthrough on future ties.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana met on Tuesday to try to resolve differences over terms for their future relations despite heated rhetoric from both the Cold War foes.

Solana was rushed straight from the airport to a ministry mansion in central Moscow where negotiations started at noon (0800 GMT). In a sign of the sensitivity of the meeting, the two sides agreed not to leak any information until the end of talks.
Interfax news agency said the talks were scheduled to last three hours but could continue longer. A joint statement was expected to be released simultaneously in Moscow and Brussels.

Both sides said they were hoping for a breakthrough to enable them to put aside disagreements over NATO's plans to expand eastwards and sign an accord in the coming weeks setting out terms for peaceful coexistence into the next century.
"The main thing is to reach a result, not to tell the world who did what to bring about the success," Interfax quoted a Russian foreign ministry source as saying on Monday.
Primakov said last week that Russia hopes to sign a partnership document with NATO on May 27 in Paris.
But both sides have been talking tough, accusing each other of doing too little to come to terms.

The main sticking point is Russia's fear that the alliance's plans to invite in former Soviet bloc countries in July will lead to a military build-up near its borders. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are the front-runners to join.
Russia is also demanding a say in some NATO decision-making.

"So far NATO has not changed enough for us not to feel a threat if the alliance's military structures approach our borders," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Mamedov, who recently held talks in Washington, as saying.

Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky, in charge of coordinating foreign policy in the Kremlin, complained on the eve of talks that some NATO members "are not showing enough desire to seek a compromise".
"Such an agreement must be reached on an equal basis, but not at all costs," he told Interfax.

In Brussels, diplomats said they were disappointed with the tough conditions laid down by Primakov when he visited Paris last week. They said he had effectively asked NATO to rule out the future military reinforcement of new alliance members.

"Solana is going to have to be very tough, we have made a generous offer which meets many Russian concerns. Whether Moscow takes it or not, enlargement is going ahead anyway," a senior Western diplomat said on Monday.
Russia has made clear it is searching for new allies to counterbalance NATO expansion.

Kremlin leaders gave a warm welcome to Indian Prime Minister H.D.Deve Gowda last month and Iranian parliamentary speeker Ali-Akbar Nateq-Nouri, who left Moscow on Monday. Chinese President Jiang Zemin is due to visit Moscow on April 22-26.

"We are against any attempts to return the world artificially to one-sided decisions on key global political and economic problems in the interests of a narrow group of states," RIA news agency quoted Primakov as saying in an interview to the Indian newspaper Hindu.
